sections.heading: ResearchStudio-Idea: An Evidence-Grounded Research-Ideation Skill Suite from ML Conference Outcomes

content.text: ResearchStudio-Idea: An Evidence-Grounded Research-Ideation Skill Suite from ML Conference Outcomes
Qihao Zhao1, Yangyu Huang2‡, Yalun Dai1,2, Lingao Xiao2,3, Jianjun Gao1, Xin Zhang2, Wenshan Wu2
Scarlett Li2, Yang He3,4, Yan Lu2, Yap Kim Hui1‡
1Nanyang Technological University 2Microsoft Research 3National University of Singapore 4CFAR, A\*STAR

LLM-based research agents have made scientific ideation easier to scale. Recent systems can retrieve papers, propose hypotheses, coordinate specialist agents, plan experiments, write code, and draft reports [[29](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib1), [40](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib2), [49](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib3), [18](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib5), [11](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib9), [25](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib6)]. Search-based methods expand the candidate space. Novelty tools make prior-art checking more explicit. This progress shifts the bottleneck. The hard question is no longer whether an LLM can produce a plausible proposal. It is whether early-stage research work can be organized into reusable skills that ground evidence, generate one defensible direction, and audit its distance from prior art before experiments begin.

ResearchStudio-Idea addresses this first-mile problem as a suite of three open skills. *Paper-Search* provides reusable literature grounding across arXiv, DBLP, OpenAlex, OpenReview, Semantic Scholar, and Crossref. *Scoop-Check* performs claim-level prior-art collision checking by decomposing a proposed novelty into problem framing, core mechanism, key insight, and application domain, then comparing those axes against retrieved prior work. *IdeaSpark* is the end-to-end skill: it composes literature grounding, bottleneck diagnosis, pattern-guided candidate construction, collision retrieval, audit, and idea-card packaging into one research-problem-to-idea-card workflow. Paper-Search and Scoop-Check are therefore not hidden implementation details; they are standalone skills that also supply reusable search and review functions inside the larger ideation loop.

The empirical center of this report is IdeaSpark because it is the point where ResearchStudio-Idea’s search, generation, and review functions must work together. We study it as *outcome-grounded skill induction* for LLM research ideation. The object we induce is an inference-time skill, not an acceptance predictor, novelty score, or paper-writing agent. The skill consists of ideation pattern cards, workflow prompts, schemas, retrieval hooks, and validators that an LLM loads while generating a structured idea. We ground it in public ML conference outcomes because those outcomes contain traces of research practice. Oral papers show cases that program committees elevated. High-citation papers show what the community reused. Rejected submissions show how similar attempts fail. The goal is to turn those traces into operational guidance, while keeping acceptance and execution outside the claim.

This report asks two questions. First, can conference outcomes be mined into a compact but usable map of ideation patterns? Second, can that map be packaged as a model-agnostic skill suite whose workflow generates and audits one research idea? We answer the first question with a 1,947-paper analysis of ICLR, ICML, and NeurIPS outcomes. We answer the second by releasing ResearchStudio-Idea’s three skills and evaluating IdeaSpark-generated ideas with blind automated judges. The evaluation is scoped to the idea stage. It does not test implementation success, human peer review, or program-committee selection.

Existing systems address important pieces of research ideation, but they leave a missing skill layer between outcome data and generation. End-to-end systems automate long research workflows [[29](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib1), [40](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib2), [49](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib3), [61](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib35)]. Multi-agent and search systems explore larger proposal spaces [[60](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib10), [17](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib12), [53](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib59), [38](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib11), [4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib13)]. Retrieval-augmented methods ground hypotheses in adjacent literature [[23](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib39), [14](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib14), [56](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib15), [8](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib60)]. Novelty tools, benchmarks, and pattern-induction methods check prior-art collision or name recurring research moves [[55](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib20), [59](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib21), [7](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib22), [43](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib23), [41](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib61), [26](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib16), [13](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib17), [22](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib18), [44](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib19)]. These components are complementary. What remains under-specified is how to turn them into interoperable skills, and how to turn conference outcomes into an executable ideation workflow: a reusable procedural object that helps an LLM organize a gap, instantiate a research strategy, distinguish it from neighboring work, and audit the proposal before implementation.

Research assistants are increasingly capable of retrieving literature, synthesizing evidence, generating candidate ideas, and iteratively refining proposals. The transition from retrieved evidence to actionable research opportunities, however, remains weakly structured. Researchers still need to decide which limitations constitute meaningful bottlenecks, which opportunities remain unresolved, and which directions are distinct enough from prior work to justify further investment.

Current evaluations of LLM-generated ideas make this gap concrete. A large blind study finds that LLM-generated NLP ideas can be judged more novel than expert ideas while being less feasible [[46](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib26)]. A follow-up execution study reports that the gap becomes sharper once ideas are carried out [[45](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib27)]. HindSight similarly finds that ideas rated as more novel by an LLM are less likely to match real future work [[19](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib29)]. These results do not imply that an idea-stage skill can solve execution. They do show that surface novelty, proposal fluency, and post-hoc novelty scoring are weak proxies for useful ideation.

A useful skill should instead expose how real papers connect a gap to a method. It should show how they assemble differentiation evidence, and how similar attempts fail before experiments begin. We call these recurring procedural objects *ideation patterns*. A pattern is not merely a label such as “decompose the problem” or “add supervision.” It must state what kind of gap it applies to, how the method is constructed, what distinguishes it from nearby prior work, what evidence makes it credible, and where similar attempts fail.

The missing middle is therefore an outcome-grounded skill layer that connects research evidence, identified bottlenecks, reusable ideation patterns, and candidate research directions. Retrieved papers expose observations, limitations, reviewer concerns, and unresolved questions. Generated proposals require strategic moves that connect those observations to plausible directions. The missing layer is the mechanism that transforms evidence into opportunities and opportunities into auditable research proposals.

We need to know how these patterns recur across ML papers, how they compose inside contributions, and how they differ across accepted, high-citation, and rejected work. We also need to know whether they can be operationalized as reusable inference-time skills. ResearchStudio-Idea addresses this missing middle as a suite, and IdeaSpark tests the strongest version of the claim: whether search, pattern-guided generation, collision checking, and audit can be composed into one faithful ideation workflow rather than another generic brainstorming prompt or novelty scorer. Section [2.6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#S2.SS6 "2.6 How IdeaSpark differs from current idea-generation methods ‣ 2 Related Work ‣ ResearchStudio-Idea: An Evidence-Grounded Research-Ideation Skill Suitefrom ML Conference Outcomes") gives the detailed comparison to current idea-generation methods.

ResearchStudio-Idea packages early-stage ideation into three reusable skills. Paper-Search supplies the literature-grounding primitive. Scoop-Check supplies the claim-level prior-art review primitive. IdeaSpark induces ideation patterns from conference outcomes and packages them as the structured end-to-end ideation skill. Given a research problem and an evidence bundle, IdeaSpark performs evidence assessment, bottleneck diagnosis, innovation-pattern retrieval, candidate construction, differentiation analysis, collision retrieval, and outcome-informed auditing. The output is not only a candidate research direction, but also the supporting rationale, historical precedents, and diagnostic evidence needed to evaluate it. Figure [2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#S1.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 1.3 Approach overview ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ ResearchStudio-Idea: An Evidence-Grounded Research-Ideation Skill Suitefrom ML Conference Outcomes") summarizes this data-to-skill flow from corpus construction to runtime use.

The empirical pipeline has four stages. First, we collect papers from ICLR, ICML, and NeurIPS using public OpenReview metadata and Semantic Scholar citation information [[34](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib50), [42](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib51)]. Each paper is labeled as Oral, High-Cited, Reject, or a combination when labels overlap. Second, we extract strategy-level innovation fields and rewrite them into domain-agnostic descriptions. This separates the methodological operation from topic vocabulary. As a result, clustering groups papers by research strategy rather than by application area. Third, we embed and cluster these strategy signatures, using a workflow inspired by scientific document representations and density-based topic discovery [[6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib41), [47](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib42), [1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib43), [12](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib44), [31](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib45), [30](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib46), [33](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib49)]. Fourth, we induce higher-level ideation patterns from the fine-grained clusters and convert each pattern into an operational card.

The resulting cards are not taxonomy labels. Each card records the research situation the pattern addresses, the structure distilled from accepted examples, the differentiating mechanism relative to nearby prior work, the evidence expectations that make the claim inspectable, and the failure modes abstracted from rejected submissions. This contrast between success and failure offers insights beyond accepted-only inductions. In the runtime skill, the cards serve two roles. They guide structured idea generation, and they provide an audit reference for checking whether a candidate preserves the intended structure, avoids known failure modes, and names plausible prior-art threats. Generation and audit share the same corpus-derived object, while the paper’s claim remains at the idea stage.

The IdeaSpark layer follows a model-agnostic, two-tier design. The runtime tier includes lean skill specification, phase prompts, schemas, retrieval hooks, and deterministic validators. The evidence tier consists of 15 ideation-pattern cards, 31 sub-pattern cards, a domain-by-pattern matrix, saturation records, and a corpus-derived failure-mode inventory. This separation follows recent skill-authoring guidance: keep the runtime lightweight, use progressive disclosure for detailed evidence, and validate phase boundaries with deterministic checks where possible [[3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib47), [39](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib40), [54](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib37), [58](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib38)]. Consequently, the skill is faithful by construction rather than by instruction. Every significant claim either traces to a retrieved record or is explicitly marked as model-supplied. Retrieval gates and deterministic validators enforce this contract rather than relying on prompt compliance (§[13.5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#S13.SS5 "13.5 Faithfulness: resisting hallucination ‣ 13 IdeaSpark Design ‣ ResearchStudio-Idea: An Evidence-Grounded Research-Ideation Skill Suitefrom ML Conference Outcomes")).
This report supports five findings:

First, the induced pattern space is compact but nontrivial. From 31 fine-grained ideation sub-patterns, the pipeline induces 15 higher-level ideation patterns. The number 15 is not a canonical ontology of ML innovation. It is the operational granularity produced by the current extraction, abstraction, embedding, clustering, and induction pipeline. Because it comes from a single Opus 4.7 induction call, an inter-prompt, inter-seed, and inter-model stability study remains future work; we expect a comparable run to land at 12–18 categories with substantial overlap.

Second, rejected and accepted papers often share the same high-level pattern space. Reject-only re-clustering maps every rejected-paper cluster back onto the existing 15-pattern vocabulary, with no out-of-taxonomy bucket. This suggests that rejected submissions are most useful as contrastive evidence about weak instantiations, failure modes, and boundary cases, not as a separate negative strategy class.

Third, multi-pattern composition is the norm. A separate paper-level multi-label pass shows that papers commonly combine several ideation patterns rather than executing a single isolated move. In this corpus, k=2k=2 is the modal composition size across Oral, HC, and Reject papers, with a 33.6%33.6\% tail at k≥3k\geq 3. This motivates the skill design choice to generate one to three pattern roles rather than selecting a single pattern as a recipe.
k≥3k\geq 3

Fourth, ideation patterns are broadly domain-covering but domain-conditional in effect. The largest patterns appear across many induced research domains, which supports the use of domain-agnostic pattern cards. Acceptance and impact profiles, however, vary by domain-pattern cell. The skill therefore treats domain statistics as audit context, not as a deterministic generation prior.

Fifth, endpoint idea quality is supported by an automated-judge study, but not by human review. An automated-judge endpoint evaluation (Section [14](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#S14 "14 Evaluation: Generated-Idea Quality and Novelty ‣ ResearchStudio-Idea: An Evidence-Grounded Research-Ideation Skill Suitefrom ML Conference Outcomes")) indicates that IdeaSpark improves generated-idea quality over no-skill and generic-skill baselines. Acceptance-level claims still require a blind human study.
This report makes three contributions.

Outcome-grounded pattern map. We provide a 1,947-paper corpus analysis spanning Oral, high-citation, and rejected papers from major ML conferences. The analysis induces 15 ideation patterns, 31 sub-patterns, and 28 research domains. It then measures pattern-level acceptance, citation, domain, conference, temporal, and multi-pattern composition profiles.

Contrastive, failure-aware pattern cards. We turn the accepted-versus-rejected contrast into card content. Each card pairs success conditions distilled from accepted work with failure modes distilled from rejected work. Accepted-only induction cannot supply this object. The empirical warrant is the reject-only mapping of §[10](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#S10 "10 Do Rejected Papers Inhabit a Different Strategy Space? ‣ ResearchStudio-Idea: An Evidence-Grounded Research-Ideation Skill Suitefrom ML Conference Outcomes"): rejected papers do not occupy a separate strategy space, so their value is as contrastive evidence about weak instantiations and boundary cases.

ResearchStudio-Idea skill suite and endpoint evaluation. We package the work as three reusable skills: Paper-Search for literature grounding, Scoop-Check for prior-art collision checking, and IdeaSpark for end-to-end idea generation and audit. We also report a blind automated evaluation of IdeaSpark-generated ideas along quality and novelty axes.

Section [2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#S2 "2 Related Work ‣ ResearchStudio-Idea: An Evidence-Grounded Research-Ideation Skill Suitefrom ML Conference Outcomes") positions ResearchStudio-Idea and IdeaSpark against recent work on LLM-based scientific discovery, ideation, novelty assessment, benchmarks, and pattern induction. Sections [3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#S3 "3 Dataset Construction ‣ ResearchStudio-Idea: An Evidence-Grounded Research-Ideation Skill Suitefrom ML Conference Outcomes")–[6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#S6 "6 Ideation-Pattern Induction ‣ ResearchStudio-Idea: An Evidence-Grounded Research-Ideation Skill Suitefrom ML Conference Outcomes") describe the dataset, extraction procedure, clustering pipeline, and ideation-pattern induction. Sections [7](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#S7 "7 Acceptance and Impact Analysis ‣ ResearchStudio-Idea: An Evidence-Grounded Research-Ideation Skill Suitefrom ML Conference Outcomes")–[9](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#S9 "9 Temporal and Conference Structure ‣ ResearchStudio-Idea: An Evidence-Grounded Research-Ideation Skill Suitefrom ML Conference Outcomes") analyze acceptance profiles, domain structure, temporal trends, and conference-level variation. Section [10](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#S10 "10 Do Rejected Papers Inhabit a Different Strategy Space? ‣ ResearchStudio-Idea: An Evidence-Grounded Research-Ideation Skill Suitefrom ML Conference Outcomes") validates the taxonomy against rejected papers. Section [11](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#S11 "11 Ablation: Embedding Model and Abstraction Stage ‣ ResearchStudio-Idea: An Evidence-Grounded Research-Ideation Skill Suitefrom ML Conference Outcomes") reports embedding and abstraction ablations. Section [12](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#S12 "12 Discussion ‣ ResearchStudio-Idea: An Evidence-Grounded Research-Ideation Skill Suitefrom ML Conference Outcomes") synthesizes the empirical takeaways. Section [13](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#S13 "13 IdeaSpark Design ‣ ResearchStudio-Idea: An Evidence-Grounded Research-Ideation Skill Suitefrom ML Conference Outcomes") specifies the IdeaSpark runtime and audit workflow within the ResearchStudio-Idea suite, and Section [14](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#S14 "14 Evaluation: Generated-Idea Quality and Novelty ‣ ResearchStudio-Idea: An Evidence-Grounded Research-Ideation Skill Suitefrom ML Conference Outcomes") reports the automated-judge evaluation of generated ideas. Section [15](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#S15 "15 Limitations ‣ ResearchStudio-Idea: An Evidence-Grounded Research-Ideation Skill Suitefrom ML Conference Outcomes") consolidates limitations and threats to validity across the corpus, skill, and evaluation. Section [16](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#S16 "16 Artifact Cards ‣ ResearchStudio-Idea: An Evidence-Grounded Research-Ideation Skill Suitefrom ML Conference Outcomes") presents the released data, model, and skill-card artifacts.

The 2024–2026 literature on LLM research-idea generation has expanded rapidly. We group it into the families most relevant to IdeaSpark and survey each below. To keep the comparison coherent, we defer direct head-to-head differentiation to §[2.6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#S2.SS6 "2.6 How IdeaSpark differs from current idea-generation methods ‣ 2 Related Work ‣ ResearchStudio-Idea: An Evidence-Grounded Research-Ideation Skill Suitefrom ML Conference Outcomes").

End-to-end systems automate the full research lifecycle. AI Scientist [[29](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib1)] drafts, implements, evaluates, and writes up research ideas in a single loop, although its output was often judged incremental. AI-Researcher [[49](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib3)] extends this direction with structured architectures and decoupled training pipelines for autonomous innovation. Agent Laboratory [[40](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib2)] starts from a human-supplied research idea and produces a research report and code, with variable human-in-the-loop control. Idea2Plan [[18](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib5)] bridges idea generation and research planning through ReAct-style scaffolding with arXiv tools. The Sakana AI Scientist v2 [[57](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib7)] adds evolutionary-search refinement, while Google AI co-scientist [[11](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib9)] uses a Gemini-based multi-agent architecture for hypothesis and proposal generation. Auto Research [[25](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib6)] spans literature review, ideation, innovation pattern, experimentation, paper writing, and rebuttal in a multi-agent framework.

A parallel critical literature documents why full-lifecycle autonomy remains fragile. Trehan et al. [[51](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib57)] distill six recurring failure modes from four autonomous ML-paper attempts: training-default bias, implementation drift under execution pressure, long-horizon context degradation, premature success declarations, thin domain knowledge, and weak experimental taste. Bisht et al. [[5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib58)] argue that current agentic scientists are not yet built for autonomy. They emphasize problem-selection bias, missing tacit laboratory knowledge, output homogenization from preference optimization, and the absence of experimental feedback loops. This line of critique motivates IdeaSpark’s narrower scope: improve the idea before downstream execution begins.

Multi-agent and search-based systems focus more directly on the ideation step. VirSci [[48](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib8)] and IRIS [[9](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib4)] model scientific teamwork through role-separated agents, such as ideators, reviewers, and retrievers. Deep Ideation [[60](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib10)] introduces an explore-expand-evolve workflow over a scientific concept network, with a critic engine trained on real reviewer feedback. Nova [[17](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib12)] adds an iterative planning-and-search loop that retrieves external knowledge to enrich each candidate and improve novelty and diversity.

Other systems make search itself the core ideation mechanism. FlowPIE [[53](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib59)] casts idea generation as a test-time evolution process driven by flow-guided Monte Carlo Tree Search over the literature. This design lets exploration and ideation co-adapt rather than run as separate stages. The multi-workflow benchmark [[38](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib11)] compares reflection-based refinement, Sakana-style evolution, Google Co-Scientist multi-agent reasoning, GPT Deep Research recursive decomposition, and Gemini multimodal long-context workflows. It finds that decomposition-based and long-context workflows reach a mean novelty of 4.17/5. Alien Science [[4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib13)] formalizes a complementary creativity gap, *cognitive availability*, and learns to sample coherent but cognitively unavailable directions from clustered “idea atoms.”

The closest line of work to ours induces innovation patterns from top-conference papers. Liu et al. [[26](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib16)] annotate Oral papers against a predefined 12-category taxonomy. MoRI [[13](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib17)] extracts *motivation*→\to*innovation pattern* pairs from ICLR 2024–2025 accepted papers. It then trains a reasoning policy through supervised fine-tuning and controllable reinforcement learning on feasibility, novelty, and effectiveness. MotivGraph-SoIQ [[22](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib18)] builds a motivational knowledge graph and pairs it with Socratic dialogue for ideation. Navigating Ideation Space [[44](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib19)] decomposes scientific ideas into conceptual representations for positioning new ideas.
→\to

A parallel paradigm grounds idea generation in knowledge graphs mined from large literature corpora. SciMuse [[14](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib14)] builds a knowledge graph from 58 million research papers. In a 100-research-group-leader evaluation, its cross-disciplinary graph paths help AI-generated ideas be perceived as novel and impactful. KG-grounded hypothesis generation [[56](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib15)] retrieves relevant graph sub-structures to constrain LLM hypothesis output and reports improved novelty and plausibility on biomedical benchmarks. Graphs of Research [[8](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib60)] turns citation structure into a training signal. It extracts a per-seed-paper citation-evolution directed acyclic graph from the 2-hop reference neighborhood and fine-tunes an LLM to generate ideas that plausibly extend it.

A separate family judges ideas rather than producing them. The first line focuses on novelty collision. NovBench [[55](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib20)] provides a large-scale benchmark for novelty evaluation, with 1,684 paper-review pairs and a four-dimensional framework covering relevance, correctness, coverage, and clarity. RINoBench [[41](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib61)] complements it with 1,381 expert-judged ideas focused on novelty judgment. It finds that LLM novelty verdicts can diverge substantially from expert gold, even when the model gives human-like rationales. We treat this as motivation for grounding novelty checks in retrieved evidence rather than model opinion. OpenNovelty [[59](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib21)] produces transparent evidence-based novelty reports for 500+ ICLR 2026 submissions. GraphMind [[7](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib22)] ties paper key elements to retrieved literature for interactive novelty assessment. Literature-Grounded Novelty Assessment / Idea Novelty Checker [[43](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib23)] uses RAG with two-stage retrieve-then-rerank and literature-grounded rationales. Scideator [[36](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib24)] combines paper facets and novelty assessment modules for human-LLM ideation. Augmenting Research Ideation with Data [[27](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib25)] integrates metadata and automated preliminary validation into ideation, reporting gains in feasibility and quality on social-science tasks.

The second line evaluates idea quality directly. Si et al. [[46](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib26)] ran a 100+-NLP-researcher blind study showing that LLM-generated ideas are rated *more novel* but *less feasible* than expert ideas. Their follow-up execution study [[45](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib27)] reports that AI ideas score significantly lower than human ideas after execution. The gap is therefore operational, not merely stylistic or novelty-related. AI Can Learn Scientific Taste [[50](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib28)] trains a taste model on accepted/rejected pairs. HindSight [[19](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib29)] evaluates LLM-generated ideas via future-citation impact. Learning to Predict Future-Aligned Research Proposals [[52](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib30)] predicts whether a candidate proposal aligns with future research directions. MIRAI [[24](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib62)] forecasts future paper impact from title and abstract, then uses that predictor to steer idea generation toward higher-impact directions.

The third line packages these judgments as standing benchmarks. IdeaBench [[15](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib31)] evaluates research idea generation against referenced-work baselines. AI Idea Bench 2025 [[35](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib32)] curates 3,495 papers from ICLR top-2% and CVPR highlights as ground truth. ResearchBench [[28](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib33)] decomposes scientific discovery into inspiration retrieval, hypothesis composition, and hypothesis ranking. NewtonBench [[62](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib34)] evaluates scientific-law discovery on 324 physics tasks with counterfactual law shifts.

Two recent surveys map the broader landscape. “From Automation to Autonomy” [[61](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib35)] organizes systems through a Tool / Analyst / Scientist taxonomy. “Towards Scientific Intelligence” [[37](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib36)] surveys architectures, benchmarks, and ethical questions. On the engineering side, Anthropic’s skill-authoring practices [[3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib47)] shape IdeaSpark’s two-tier design: progressive disclosure, a lean top-level specification, deterministic routines for repetitive steps, and schema-validated phase boundaries. The embedding and clustering substrate is described where it is used, in §[6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#S6 "6 Ideation-Pattern Induction ‣ ResearchStudio-Idea: An Evidence-Grounded Research-Ideation Skill Suitefrom ML Conference Outcomes") and §[11](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#S11 "11 Ablation: Embedding Model and Abstraction Stage ‣ ResearchStudio-Idea: An Evidence-Grounded Research-Ideation Skill Suitefrom ML Conference Outcomes").

children.heading: 2.6 How IdeaSpark differs from current idea-generation methods

content.text: Current idea-generation methods fall into three families. End-to-end “AI scientist” systems automate the full research lifecycle. Search-based systems generate many candidates and filter them with learned novelty, taste, or impact signals. Pattern- and knowledge-graph-induction methods mine accepted papers or large literature graphs for reusable structure. IdeaSpark draws ingredients from all three families: pattern induction, an accept/reject contrast, and retrieval-grounded generation. Its distinguishing move is to bind these ingredients onto one object.

That object is the non-parametric, data-induced pattern card. The same card that helps select a move for a bottleneck is also used to audit the generated candidate. This differs from searching a candidate space and ranking ideas by a learned signal. It also differs from fitting a parametric motivation→\tomethod policy, where generation and checking can become separate procedures.
→\to

Three properties follow from this design. First, the cards are induced from a three-way Oral / HC / Reject contrast, so they carry an explicit *failure* signal that accepted-only induction and concept-level knowledge graphs do not. Second, the skill stops at one reviewer-facing idea card rather than running the full research lifecycle. This choice reflects the premise that idea quality is an upstream bottleneck for many downstream failures. Third, the audit checks the candidate against the corpus-derived failure modes of the pattern that produced it, together with retrieved prior art. The knowledge that generates an idea and the knowledge that checks it are therefore one object, not two disconnected models. Execution-level gaps are surfaced rather than masked by surface novelty.

We collect papers from ICLR, ICML, and NeurIPS for 2021–2025. Collection uses the OpenReview API [[34](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib50)] (v1 for ICLR 2021–2023; v2 for ICLR 2024+, ICML 2023+, and NeurIPS 2023+) and Semantic Scholar citation metadata [[42](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib51)]. ICLR 2020 is excluded from this release because its review-data schema differs from later years. For each paper, we retain the title, abstract, author list, OpenReview id, decision string, available review fields, available meta-review, and Semantic Scholar citation count. The review fields include rating, confidence, soundness, contribution, summary, strengths, weaknesses, and questions.

The three labels operationalize the contrast at the heart of this work. Oral marks what program committees most value. High-Cited marks what the community adopts. Reject supplies the failure signal that accepted-only induction cannot provide. Each paper receives one or more labels, and labels may overlap. In this corpus, 49 papers are simultaneously Oral and High-Cited.
Oral (1,014 papers): papers whose venue decision is Oral, marking program-committee preference.

We use H​CallHC\_{\mathrm{all}} for citation-label coverage and H​CdisjointHC\_{\mathrm{disjoint}} when analyses need mutually exclusive Oral, HC, and Reject classes.

The per-venue counts reflect two independent factors.

First, venue openness: ICLR is OpenReview-native and publishes both accept and reject decisions with full review threads. Its Reject pool is therefore the deepest. ICML and NeurIPS expose decisions on OpenReview only from 2023 onward. ICML 2023–2024 in particular released very few rejected submissions, which is why those rows show 0–3 in the Reject column.

Second, review accessibility: even when a decision is published, the meta-review and reviewer comments may be withheld or formatted such that automatic parsing fails. This is why metadata coverage (Section [3.2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#S3.SS2 "3.2 Metadata coverage ‣ 3 Dataset Construction ‣ ResearchStudio-Idea: An Evidence-Grounded Research-Ideation Skill Suitefrom ML Conference Outcomes")) shows only 340 of the 1,947 papers carrying a meta-review, even though all 1,947 have decisions.

Finally, NeurIPS 2025 contributes no HC papers. As the most recent venue (December 2025), its citation counts had not accumulated enough at collection time for even a top-10 cut to be meaningful. These asymmetries do not affect the clustering stage, but we treat them carefully in the quantitative analysis (Section [7](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#S7 "7 Acceptance and Impact Analysis ‣ ResearchStudio-Idea: An Evidence-Grounded Research-Ideation Skill Suitefrom ML Conference Outcomes")).

After merging and deduplicating by OpenReview submission id, 1,947 unique papers remain. All 1,947 carry the eight base fields. The four abstracted fields (Section [4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#S4 "4 Two-Stage Innovation-Signature Extraction ‣ ResearchStudio-Idea: An Evidence-Grounded Research-Ideation Skill Suitefrom ML Conference Outcomes")) are populated with non-empty content for 1,891 papers. The remaining 56 papers are dropped from the embedding pool (§[5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#S5 "5 Unsupervised Pattern Discovery ‣ ResearchStudio-Idea: An Evidence-Grounded Research-Ideation Skill Suitefrom ML Conference Outcomes")).

Coverage of the initial merged metadata varies by field. In total, 1,074 papers carry the full abstract, 716 carry parsed reviews, 682 carry an extracted introduction, and 340 carry a meta-review. For card generation, we run a separate review-recovery pass over public OpenReview threads. The resulting card-level review-evidence coverage is reported in §[12](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#S12 "12 Discussion ‣ ResearchStudio-Idea: An Evidence-Grounded Research-Ideation Skill Suitefrom ML Conference Outcomes"). Papers without recoverable review text are still included in signature extraction. Their review-derived fields, however, are treated as low-evidence auxiliary fields rather than evidence grounded in reviewer text.

Throughout this paper, we reference corpus papers by an internal identifier of the form <VENUE>\_<YEAR>\_<NNNN>. Examples include ICLR\_2022\_0094 and NeurIPS\_2023\_0753. Each identifier resolves uniquely to an OpenReview submission via the openreview\_id field in data/dataset/all\_records\_full.json. After consulting the dataset, a paper can be looked up at https://openreview.net/forum?id=<openreview\_id>.

Of the 1,947 corpus papers, approximately 1,088 are referenced at least once in this report. They usually appear as evidence under a methodology card’s success-condition or failure-mode list. We do not include all corpus papers as bibliography entries. A complete corpus bibliography would obscure the second-order related-work citations that constitute Section [2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#S2 "2 Related Work ‣ ResearchStudio-Idea: An Evidence-Grounded Research-Ideation Skill Suitefrom ML Conference Outcomes"). The prepared dataset is therefore the authoritative bibliographic resolution layer for any paper\_id appearing in this report.

When a specific corpus paper is discussed substantively in body text, we provide a proper bibliography entry. Examples include the diffusion-ELBO paper [[20](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib52)] = NeurIPS\_2023\_0753, LP-FT [[21](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib53)] = ICLR\_2022\_0094, the DP continual-observation paper [[16](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib54)] = ICML\_2023\_0551, EigenGame [[10](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib55)] = ICLR\_2021\_0018, and SAM-as-Bayes [[32](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib56)] = ICLR\_2023\_0331.

To convert each paper into a form suitable for strategy-level clustering, we extract a twelve-field *innovation signature*. Eight base fields capture the paper in its own terms. Four describe the innovation mechanism, and four record review and outcome signals. A second stage rewrites the four mechanism fields into domain-agnostic form. Only these four rewritten fields are embedded for clustering. The eight base fields are retained for extraction and later card evidence.

For Stage 1, we feed Claude Sonnet 4.6 [[2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#bib.bib48)] the paper’s title, available abstract, available introduction, available reviews, and available meta-review. Introductions are extracted from the PDF when recoverable. The model then returns the following structured fields:

1. 1. innovation\_approach: one sentence describing *how* this paper innovates as a reasoning strategy. 2. 2. key\_step: the single most critical reasoning step from diagnosis to solution. 3. 3. why\_non\_obvious: the cognitive barrier that blocked others from this approach. 4. 4. trigger\_condition: domain-agnostic situation where this strategy applies, phrased as “When X, apply Y to achieve Z.” 5. 5. reviewer\_praise: three specific points the reviewers praised. 6. 6. reviewer\_concern: three specific reviewer concerns. 7. 7. acceptance\_signal: one sentence explaining what made the paper Oral / cited / rejected. 8. 8. contribution\_type: one of {theoretical, methodological, empirical, benchmark, system}.

The first four fields are the most strategy-bearing, so Stage 2 rewrites only those. The last four supply review and outcome evidence used later in card construction. Extraction runs under a JSON schema that enforces non-empty lists of length 3 for the two review-derived fields. All 1,947 papers pass Stage 1 extraction.

A direct embedding of paper descriptions tends to latch onto domain nouns, such as “Transformer”, “diffusion”, “image”, or “molecule”. This produces topic clusters rather than strategy clusters. We address this failure mode with a second Claude Sonnet 4.6 pass. It rewrites the first four base fields into strategy-only equivalents. The prompt instructs the model to replace domain nouns with generic placeholders, adopt imperative phrasing (“Audit …”, “Transfer …”, “Design …”), preserve the mechanism, and drop application detail. The resulting four fields are:

1. 1. abstract\_strategy ←\leftarrow innovation\_approach 2. 2. abstract\_key\_step ←\leftarrow key\_step 3. 3. abstract\_why\_non\_obvious ←\leftarrow why\_non\_obvious 4. 4. abstract\_trigger\_condition ←\leftarrow trigger\_condition

A representative contrast illustrates the shift. For the paper *High Fidelity Speech Synthesis with Adversarial Networks*, innovation\_approach reads “They solved a domain transfer problem by borrowing the PatchGAN multi-scale discriminator strategy from image GANs and re-instantiating it at multiple temporal windows in audio, adding conditioning signals to close the fidelity gap”. The corresponding abstract\_strategy reads “Transfer a multi-scale discrimination strategy from one data modality to another by re-instantiating it at the appropriate domain-specific granularity, then add conditioning signals to close the remaining fidelity gap.” The generic version is what we feed into the embedding model.

children.heading: What “unclustered” actually means (and why we don’t call it “noise”).

content.text: HDBSCAN normally labels points outside any density peak as “noise”. We instead use “unclustered” because the label is geometric, not substantive. It marks where a paper sits in the embedding; it does not mean the strategy is weak, idiosyncratic, or outside the framework.

The flagged 47.7%47.7\% are *not* strategy-empty. All 1,8911{,}891 embedded papers carry full content in the four abstract\_\* fields, and the unclustered and clustered groups have comparable median lengths. The label reflects embedding geometry at the chosen mcs threshold. A paper lands “unclustered” when its strategy embedding falls between two or three modal clusters, often because it executes several ideation patterns in roughly equal measure. In short, “unclustered” means *between modal clusters*, not *outside the strategy space*. The 15-pattern framework works at the paper level through independent multi-label tagging (§[6.5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#S6.SS5 "6.5 Paper-level multi-label ideation pattern assignment ‣ 6 Ideation-Pattern Induction ‣ ResearchStudio-Idea: An Evidence-Grounded Research-Ideation Skill Suitefrom ML Conference Outcomes")), so it covers unclustered and clustered papers equally.
Cluster sizes (excluding unclustered) range from 13 (the smallest valid size) to 86, with mean 31.9 and median 22. The five largest clusters are:

* • C02 (n=86n{=}86): *Controlled Diagnostic Construction with One-Variable-Isolated Items*, under *Design a Confound-Isolating Diagnostic*. * • C18 (n=82n{=}82): *Substrate Adaptation Across Modalities for a Mature Recipe*, under *Unify Heterogeneous Inputs into One Space*. * • C06 (n=59n{=}59): *Probabilistic-Objective Unification via Equivalence Proof*, under *Prove Equivalence to Unify*. * • C14 (n=50n{=}50): *All-Pairs Attention Operator Replacement*, under *Substitute the Operator or Representation*. * • C05 (n=50n{=}50): *Identifiability-Theorem Pivot on the Limiting Assumption*, under *Audit and Pivot an Assumption*.

Each cluster is automatically labeled by an Opus 4.7 pass. The pass reads the cluster’s eight centroid-nearest representative papers and produces a 2–6 word label plus a one-sentence description. A second Opus 4.7 pass then produces a level-2 *disambiguation card* for each cluster. The resulting tactic-level patterns are used in §[6.3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#S6.SS3 "6.3 Multi-strategy assignments ‣ 6 Ideation-Pattern Induction ‣ ResearchStudio-Idea: An Evidence-Grounded Research-Ideation Skill Suitefrom ML Conference Outcomes"). Each disambiguation card has six panels:

1. 1. *tactical\_pattern*: the cluster’s specific reasoning move at the granularity below the level-1 ideation pattern. 2. 2. *Step-by-Step*: a 5-step abstract structural-move recipe distilled from the cluster’s accepted examples, with reject-derived boundaries embedded. 3. 3. *differentiation\_within\_parent*: what distinguishes this cluster from its siblings under the same parent. 4. 4. *when\_to\_pick\_this\_one*: the situational trigger conditions under which this sub-pattern is the right choice. 5. 5. *tactical\_failure\_mode*: the cluster-specific failure shape that recurs in its Reject papers. 6. 6. *Examples*: a set of *paper-agnostic* Oral and Reject lessons. No per-paper citations are used. The lessons are abstract distillations of the cluster’s success and failure shapes, so that Phase 2.2 generation applies the abstract pattern to a new gap rather than mimicking specific papers.

content.text: *Oral-safe* does not mean “preferred”; *Reject-warn* does not mean “forbidden”. They are descriptive risk statistics with limited sample sizes. They are also sensitive to year, conference, and topic saturation. A Reject-warn cluster’s rejected papers may have failed on execution rather than tactic choice. We therefore expose these flags to human artifact readers and to the audit layer as informational risk signals. We do not gate retrieval, generation, or recommendation on them. A user whose problem genuinely matches a Reject-warn cluster’s tactic can still proceed, but the sub-pattern card informs them of the documented failure modes.

Fine-grained ideation sub-patterns answer “what specific move did this paper make?” They do not answer the higher-level question: “what kind of move is that?” To induce that level, we ask Claude Opus 4.7 to build a Level-1 ideation-pattern taxonomy from the 31 clusters. The prompt imposes four constraints. The taxonomy must contain 6–18 entries. Each entry must describe a reusable reasoning strategy rather than a domain or venue. Each entry must include a definition, an operational signature, and a when-to-apply clause. Finally, every cluster must map to one primary ideation pattern, with an optional secondary pattern.

Opus returns a 15-ideation pattern taxonomy (Table [3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#S6.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 6 Ideation-Pattern Induction ‣ ResearchStudio-Idea: An Evidence-Grounded Research-Ideation Skill Suitefrom ML Conference Outcomes")) and a 31-cluster mapping in a single structured call. We make no edits to either. The 15 ideation patterns are:

Each ideation pattern is specified at the level needed for use in the skill, with its full definition, operational signature, and when-to-apply clause given in the per-pattern card.

The 15 ideation patterns are *not* mutually exclusive categories. Several pairs naturally overlap. *Audit and Pivot an Assumption* can overlap with *Prove Equivalence to Unify*, because an equivalence proof often relaxes a load-bearing assumption. *Substitute the Operator or Representation* can overlap with *Encode Structure by Construction*, because a structured operator both substitutes and encodes. *Manufacture the Supervisory Signal* can overlap with *Design a Property-Targeting Pretext Objective*, because the latter is a structured form of the former.

The cluster-level mapping forces one primary pattern per cluster for organization. The papers themselves often execute several operators in composition, and the paper-level multi-label tagging in §[6.5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#S6.SS5 "6.5 Paper-level multi-label ideation pattern assignment ‣ 6 Ideation-Pattern Induction ‣ ResearchStudio-Idea: An Evidence-Grounded Research-Ideation Skill Suitefrom ML Conference Outcomes") confirms this empirically. The right reading is therefore compositional: the 15 patterns are ideation operators, and a paper is represented as a composition of operators rather than assigned to one exclusive class.

children.heading: A note on small-sample ideation patterns.

content.text: Three ideation patterns have small per-paper-primary populations under cluster-level inheritance: *Adapt by Conditioning, Not Retraining* (n=18n{=}18), *Characterize a Limit, Then Surpass It* (n=15n{=}15), and *Design a Property-Targeting Pretext Objective* (n=15n{=}15). These are valid operators because the underlying clusters are statistically distinct in embedding space. They are also low-support operators: their per-pattern acceptance statistics rest on thin evidence and should not be used as strong recommendation priors. The corresponding analytical cards therefore carry an internal confidence: low flag.

The runtime prompt cards do not expose raw counts or confidence flags to the model, because doing so induced distribution-bias homogenization toward high-nn patterns in earlier designs. Low-support patterns remain available when the user’s problem genuinely fits them. They are neither privileged nor down-weighted by the skill’s selection step. The corpus-side flag is retained here for analytical transparency.
nn

The ideation pattern names use compact technical phrasing for analytical precision: for example, *Audit and Pivot an Assumption* and *Substitute the Operator or Representation*. Each pattern also has a *plain-language alias* for user-facing skill output. This keeps the framework legible to non-specialists. Examples include *Audit and Pivot an Assumption* →\to “Audit the load-bearing assumption and pivot”, *Reframe as a Solvable Object* →\to “Reformulate the unsolved as a solvable object”, and *Substitute the Operator or Representation* →\to “Substitute the operator or representation”.

A definition and operational signature tell a researcher *what* an ideation pattern is. They do not explain *when it lands and when it fails*. To capture that distinction, we run a second Opus 4.7 pass for each ideation pattern. The input includes all Oral, HC, and Reject papers assigned to the pattern, their four abstracted fields, and the available review and meta-review evidence. Review evidence is recovered for 83% of the corpus overall; details are in §[12](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#S12 "12 Discussion ‣ ResearchStudio-Idea: An Evidence-Grounded Research-Ideation Skill Suitefrom ML Conference Outcomes"). The pass returns a structured card with seven panels:

1. 1. *success\_conditions*: cross-Oral patterns of what makes the pattern land. 2. 2. *failure\_modes*: cross-Reject patterns of how it fails. 3. 3. *oral\_reject\_gap*: the prose contrast between the two pools. 4. 4. *oral\_hc\_gap*: the prose contrast between PC-favored and community-favored execution. 5. 5. *reviewer\_expectations*: bullets tagged by provenance ([oral\_reviews], [reject\_reviews], [both]). 6. 6. *cognitive\_barriers*: the field-level blind spots that make the pattern non-obvious. 7. 7. *representative\_examples*: 6–8 paper-anchored exemplars (Oral and Reject), each with a one-line lesson.
*success\_conditions*: cross-Oral patterns of what makes the pattern land.
*failure\_modes*: cross-Reject patterns of how it fails.
*oral\_reject\_gap*: the prose contrast between the two pools.
*oral\_hc\_gap*: the prose contrast between PC-favored and community-favored execution.
*reviewer\_expectations*: bullets tagged by provenance ([oral\_reviews], [reject\_reviews], [both]).
*cognitive\_barriers*: the field-level blind spots that make the pattern non-obvious.
*representative\_examples*: 6–8 paper-anchored exemplars (Oral and Reject), each with a one-line lesson.

Evidence-bearing fields must cite paper IDs. This rule applies to *success\_conditions*, *failure\_modes*, *oral\_reject\_gap*, *oral\_hc\_gap*, *reviewer\_expectations*, and *representative\_examples*. The model is also instructed to set confidence=low when sample sizes or review coverage fall below thresholds, and to refuse the Oral-vs-HC contrast when nH​C<5n\_{HC}<5.

The 15 resulting cards are the operational substrate of the skill. Definitions, operational signatures, and when-to-apply clauses support Phase 2.1 pattern fit. Sub-pattern tactical recipes support Phase 2.2 instantiation. Failure modes, Oral-vs-Reject gaps, representative examples, and reviewer expectations support Phase 3 audit and Phase 4 explanation. They are not used as acceptance-rate priors or ranking signals.

The cards’ Examples panel surfaces *paper-agnostic Oral and Reject lessons*: bullets distilled from the cluster’s acceptance pool, without per-paper citations. This design keeps Phase 2.2 focused on applying the abstract pattern to a new gap rather than mimicking any single corpus paper. App. [D](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#A4 "Appendix D Exemplar Ideation Pattern and Sub-pattern Card ‣ ResearchStudio-Idea: An Evidence-Grounded Research-Ideation Skill Suitefrom ML Conference Outcomes") reproduces the *Audit and Pivot an Assumption* card—paired with one of its sub-pattern cards—as a high-coverage corpus-to-card example.

* • Cluster-level coverage: 989 of 989 clustered papers (100%100\% of clustered; 52%52\% of the 1,891-paper embedding pool) receive a primary ideation pattern by inheritance from their ideation sub-pattern. Every cluster maps to exactly one of the 15 primary patterns; there is no out-of-taxonomy residual. * • Paper-level multi-label coverage: the independent multi-label tagging pass (§[6.5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#S6.SS5 "6.5 Paper-level multi-label ideation pattern assignment ‣ 6 Ideation-Pattern Induction ‣ ResearchStudio-Idea: An Evidence-Grounded Research-Ideation Skill Suitefrom ML Conference Outcomes")) assigns one or more ideation pattern labels to *all* papers including the 902902 HDBSCAN-unclustered ones. The 15-ideation pattern framework therefore covers the corpus completely at the paper level, even though only 52%52\% of papers are assignable via cluster-level inheritance.

The distribution has a long tail. By cluster-level primary count, the top three ideation patterns account for 384 papers: *Audit and Pivot an Assumption* (n=181n{=}181), *Substitute the Operator or Representation* (n=109n{=}109), and *Liberate a Fixed Generative Component* (n=94n{=}94). The bottom three account for 48 papers: *Adapt by Conditioning* (n=18n{=}18), *Characterize a Limit* (n=15n{=}15), and *Design a Property-Targeting Pretext Objective* (n=15n{=}15). This is the long-tail signature of an inductively derived taxonomy. Many innovations use a small number of deeply worked strategies; a smaller tail uses rare but still coherent operators.

Figure [5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#S6.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 6.2 Coverage and granularity ‣ 6 Ideation-Pattern Induction ‣ ResearchStudio-Idea: An Evidence-Grounded Research-Ideation Skill Suitefrom ML Conference Outcomes") visualizes the hierarchy with three concentric rings. The inner ring shows the 15 ideation patterns, sized by paper count. The middle ring subdivides each pattern into its constituent sub-clusters, 31 in total, tinted with the parent pattern’s color. The outer band encodes each pattern’s Oral acceptance rate on a light→\rightarrowdark gray scale. Two empirical observations follow.

(i) Methodology fragmentation is uneven across patterns, but the taxonomy is not over-split. *Audit and Pivot an Assumption* decomposes into 6 sub-clusters. *Substitute the Operator or Representation* decomposes into 4. *Reframe as a Solvable Object*, *Manufacture the Supervisory Signal*, *Encode Structure by Construction*, and *Liberate a Fixed Generative Component* decompose into 3 each. The remaining 9 patterns are single-cluster patterns, which indicates tactically coherent moves that the abstraction does not split further. The 6-cluster decomposition under *Audit and Pivot* reflects substantively different audit-pivot moves, such as identifiability-theorem pivots, distributional-assumption pivots, and sufficiency-bound pivots.

(ii) Cluster sizes are tight and well-supported. Cluster sizes range from 13 to 86 (mean 31.9, median 22). Of the 31 clusters, only 2 are small (n<15n<15); the corresponding tactical cards are auto-flagged as confidence: low. The tight size distribution corresponds to a high silhouette (0.5840.584).

This subsection reports the cluster-level view of multi-strategy composition. This view is deliberately limited: the cluster-level mapping caps each paper at *primary + secondary*. The deeper paper-level multi-label view in §[6.5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#S6.SS5 "6.5 Paper-level multi-label ideation pattern assignment ‣ 6 Ideation-Pattern Induction ‣ ResearchStudio-Idea: An Evidence-Grounded Research-Ideation Skill Suitefrom ML Conference Outcomes") recovers the true modal composition, including the 902 HDBSCAN-unclustered papers excluded here. It should be read as the authoritative composition analysis.

Paper-level coverage of the secondary slot. The cluster-level (primary, secondary) assignment propagates to papers. Of the 989 clustered papers, 729729 (73.7%73.7\%) carry both a primary and a non-trivial secondary, while 260260 (26.3%26.3\%) carry only a primary. The 902902 HDBSCAN-unclustered papers are excluded from these cluster-level statistics and assigned later by multi-label tagging in §[6.5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#S6.SS5 "6.5 Paper-level multi-label ideation pattern assignment ‣ 6 Ideation-Pattern Induction ‣ ResearchStudio-Idea: An Evidence-Grounded Research-Ideation Skill Suitefrom ML Conference Outcomes"). Multi-strategy assignment is therefore the norm among coherently clustered papers.

Two cluster-level signals are worth stating because both fall outside the Oral-enriched paper-level ranking in §[6.5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#S6.SS5 "6.5 Paper-level multi-label ideation pattern assignment ‣ 6 Ideation-Pattern Induction ‣ ResearchStudio-Idea: An Evidence-Grounded Research-Ideation Skill Suitefrom ML Conference Outcomes") (Table [6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#S6.T6 "Table 6 ‣ Top combinations under multi-label tagging. ‣ 6.5 Paper-level multi-label ideation pattern assignment ‣ 6 Ideation-Pattern Induction ‣ ResearchStudio-Idea: An Evidence-Grounded Research-Ideation Skill Suitefrom ML Conference Outcomes")). First, the clearest reject-enriched combination is *architectural operator substitution* ++ *heterogeneous decomposition* (−17.9-17.9 pp from the 58.4%58.4\% baseline), followed by *algebraic equivalence unification* ++ *operator substitution* (−8.4-8.4 pp). The likely failure mode is stacked unresolved tradeoffs: a more expressive operator is asked to absorb multi-population heterogeneity, so reviewers read the operator as the architecture rather than as a controlled inductive bias. Second, composition itself tracks acceptance. The 729729 paired papers reach pO=58.2%p\_{O}=58.2\% (366/263366/263), essentially the 58.4%58.4\% baseline. The 260260 single-pattern papers reach only 52.7%52.7\% (116/104116/104, −5.7-5.7 pp). A single-primary cluster tends to be a lone tactical move, whose acceptance signal is weaker than a deliberately composed pair.

Why do certain ideation pattern pairs combine often? The OpenAI text-embedding-3-large embedding gives a direct geometric measure. children.heading: What multi-label tagging implies for the skill.

content.text: The skill treats ideation-pattern composition as 1–3 entries per generated idea, with k=2k=2 as the empirically supported default. For each composed pattern, it draws success and failure conditions from the ideation-pattern cards in §[6.1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#S6.SS1 "6.1 From definition to operational card ‣ 6 Ideation-Pattern Induction ‣ ResearchStudio-Idea: An Evidence-Grounded Research-Ideation Skill Suitefrom ML Conference Outcomes"). The combination statistics in Table [6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#S6.T6 "Table 6 ‣ Top combinations under multi-label tagging. ‣ 6.5 Paper-level multi-label ideation pattern assignment ‣ 6 Ideation-Pattern Induction ‣ ResearchStudio-Idea: An Evidence-Grounded Research-Ideation Skill Suitefrom ML Conference Outcomes") are surfaced only as context through the candidate’s innovation\_pattern\_landscape block. That block shows the area’s pattern usage alongside the candidate’s chosen composition, so the user can see where the idea sits in the empirical distribution.

Pattern selection itself happens upstream by structural fit to the bottleneck in Phase 2.1, not by composition-rate priors. Loading priors at generation time was tested in an earlier design and removed because it induced distribution-bias homogenization across runs. children.heading: 8.3 Ideation-pattern breadth: how domain-agnostic is each pattern?

content.text: For the skill to judge whether a pattern is plausible in a user’s area, it needs each pattern’s domain footprint. Figure [11](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#S8.F11 "Figure 11 ‣ 8.3 Ideation-pattern breadth: how domain-agnostic is each pattern? ‣ 8 Domain Distribution and Ideation-Pattern Breadth ‣ ResearchStudio-Idea: An Evidence-Grounded Research-Ideation Skill Suitefrom ML Conference Outcomes") plots, for each ideation pattern, the number of domains it touches and the share of its papers concentrated in its largest domain.
≥5\geq 5
Three observations:

(i) Diagnostic and framing patterns reach the entire field. *Audit and Pivot an Assumption* and *Reframe as a Solvable Object* each have ≥5\geq 5 papers in all 28 domains. *Decompose for Differentiated Treatment* reaches 27 domains. These three are also the highest-volume patterns in the multi-label distribution, with 10081008, 527527, and 529529 papers respectively under tagging. They also anchor the Oral-enriched multi-label combinations in Table [6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#S6.T6 "Table 6 ‣ Top combinations under multi-label tagging. ‣ 6.5 Paper-level multi-label ideation pattern assignment ‣ 6 Ideation-Pattern Induction ‣ ResearchStudio-Idea: An Evidence-Grounded Research-Ideation Skill Suitefrom ML Conference Outcomes"). Breadth, volume, and acceptance signal therefore co-occur.
≥5\geq 5

(ii) Construction-level patterns are still broad, but more concentrated. *Encode Structure by Construction* reaches 2525 domains, *Liberate a Fixed Generative Component* reaches 2525, *Manufacture the Supervisory Signal* reaches 2323, and *Substitute the Operator or Representation* reaches 2222. These patterns depend on a specific architectural choice or generative inductive bias. They appear across most of the field, but with clearer domain-modal anchors. Generative redesign concentrates in Diffusion, Flow & Score Models, and operator substitution concentrates in Sequence Modeling & Architectures.

(iii) Domain-narrow patterns are not necessarily Reject-prone. *Relax Discrete Search to Continuous* touches 99 domains, *Unify Heterogeneous Inputs into One Space* touches 1111, and *Characterize a Limit, Then Surpass It* touches 1212. The first two are narrow because their operational substrates exist only in some subfields: discrete-search-amenable problems and cross-modal alignment scaffolds. *Characterize a Limit, Then Surpass It* is also narrow, but it is the cleanest cross-domain Oral signal we observe (§[8.2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#S8.SS2 "8.2 Domain × ideation pattern heatmap ‣ 8 Domain Distribution and Ideation-Pattern Breadth ‣ ResearchStudio-Idea: An Evidence-Grounded Research-Ideation Skill Suitefrom ML Conference Outcomes")). Its narrowness reflects a prerequisite. The field must already have produced a formal limit characterization, which is not true everywhere.

We do not report a per-domain temporal slice. Conditioning on (domain ×\times year ×\times pattern) leaves only 1–3 papers per cell for smaller domains, which is too thin for a quantitative claim. The skill also does not rely on such aggregate slices. Its Phase 2.1 saturation read is computed live from each run’s Phase 0 retrieval (§[9](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#S9 "9 Temporal and Conference Structure ‣ ResearchStudio-Idea: An Evidence-Grounded Research-Ideation Skill Suitefrom ML Conference Outcomes")), so domain-specific saturation is read from the actual retrieved literature rather than from coarse dataset bins.

children.heading: How the skill uses these trend signals.

content.text: These corpus-wide temporal verdicts are descriptive context only. The skill never loads them as generation priors. Instead, Phase 1 reads pattern saturation live from each run’s own retrieved literature (§[13](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#S13 "13 IdeaSpark Design ‣ ResearchStudio-Idea: An Evidence-Grounded Research-Ideation Skill Suitefrom ML Conference Outcomes")).

Figure [13](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#S9.F13 "Figure 13 ‣ 9.2 Conference preferences ‣ 9 Temporal and Conference Structure ‣ ResearchStudio-Idea: An Evidence-Grounded Research-Ideation Skill Suitefrom ML Conference Outcomes") reports each pattern’s share within each venue, measured as the percentage of that venue’s papers carrying the pattern under multi-label tagging. Three venue signatures emerge.

ICML over-indexes on assumption-audit and limit-characterization. *Audit and Pivot an Assumption* reaches 56.2%56.2\% share at ICML versus 52.4%52.4\% elsewhere, a +3.8+3.8 pp lift. *Characterize a Limit, Then Surpass It* reaches 5.7%5.7\% versus 4.3%4.3\%, a +1.4+1.4 pp lift. Both patterns are diagnostic or theoretical, consistent with ICML’s preference for sharply bounded analytical contributions.

ICLR over-indexes on construction-side moves. *Encode Structure by Construction* reaches 20.6%20.6\% versus 16.2%16.2\% elsewhere (+4.4+4.4 pp). *Liberate a Fixed Generative Component* reaches 16.2%16.2\% versus 13.3%13.3\% (+3.0+3.0 pp). ICLR also under-indexes on *Prove Equivalence to Unify* (−2.7-2.7 pp) and *Audit and Pivot an Assumption* (−4.5-4.5 pp). The venue signature favors architectural and representational construction over algebraic unification.

NeurIPS over-indexes on heterogeneity-driven decomposition and supervisory-signal engineering. *Decompose for Differentiated Treatment* reaches 31.4%31.4\% versus 26.8%26.8\% elsewhere (+4.7+4.7 pp). *Manufacture the Supervisory Signal* reaches 18.0%18.0\% versus 14.3%14.3\% (+3.7+3.7 pp). NeurIPS under-indexes on *Design a Confound-Isolating Diagnostic* (−4.0-4.0 pp). The venue signature is broadly systems-level composition plus invented supervision, consistent with its empirical bias toward large-experiment papers.

These venue signatures are quantified per pattern. The skill surfaces them only as audit context for the Phase 4 idea card, so the user can see the venue prior alongside the candidate’s chosen pattern composition.

children.heading: 10 Do Rejected Papers Inhabit a Different Strategy Space?

content.text: A natural concern is that clustering Oral, HC, and Reject papers in one space may force Reject papers into clusters defined by accepted work. If rejected papers used *different* strategies, the induced ideation patterns would under-represent them. We test this directly. The result is negative: rejected work clusters within the same 15-pattern taxonomy rather than in a strategy space of its own.

We re-run the embedding+clustering pipeline on the 711 Reject papers that carry full abstract\_\* fields. Of the 722 Reject papers, 11 lack one of the four fields. We keep the UMAP hyperparameters fixed (n​\_​components=5n\\_\text{components}{=}5, n​\_​neighbors=10n\\_\text{neighbors}{=}10, cosine metric, seed 42). We also keep HDBSCAN fixed at min⁡\_​cluster\_size=10\min\\_\text{cluster\\_size}{=}10 with cluster\_selection\_method=leaf. This configuration produces 13 Reject-only clusters, with an unclustered fraction of 40.5%40.5\% (288/711288/711).

We then map each Reject-only cluster to its nearest main-pattern centroid in the original 3,0723{,}072-dimensional text-embedding-3-large space (§[6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.04439v1#S6 "6 Ideation-Pattern Induction ‣ ResearchStudio-Idea: An Evidence-Grounded Research-Ideation Skill Suitefrom ML Conference Outcomes")). All 13 clusters land within 0.8970.897–0.9860.986 cosine of their assigned primary. In total, 11 of the 15 main patterns receive at least one Reject-only cluster. No Reject-only cluster requires an out-of-taxonomy label.

Four main patterns receive *no* Reject-only mapping: *Adapt by Conditioning, Not Retraining*, *Characterize a Limit, Then Surpass It*, *Design a Property-Targeting Pretext Objective*, and *Encode Structure by Construction*. Three are small-sample patterns (n≤18n\leq 18 each), and one is a constructively encoded pattern. The empirical reading is that Reject papers do not form a separate strategic space.
